items.quote: A Secret indeed is to be concealed, it belongs onely to God to reveale it
items.note: The author states that a secret is to be concealed and that revealing it belongs to God alone.

items.quote: if it be disclosed, commonly it exposeth to death, or prison, or reproach
items.note: Disclosing the secret is said to bring danger to the one who discloses it; this is his reason for concealment.

items.name: Lully; Arnold, Zachary of Paris
items.quote: Lully; Arnold, Zachary of Paris, and others, are witnesses hereof
items.note: Named persons are cited as witnesses of the dangers of disclosure.

items.quote: The true Hermetick Phylosophers took an Oath that they would follow the footsteps of their fathers and masters
items.note: The philosophers are bound by an oath to keep to their masters' way; secrecy under oath.

items.quote: not by any teinerity defile the virginity of Nature
items.note: A figure: Nature's virginity, kept since the beginning of the world, is what the oath protects; not meant plainly.

items.quote: yet have they bequeathed their secrets to their sworn disciples
items.note: The secrets are passed on, but only to sworn disciples made worthy by nature or education; meant for some readers only.

items.quote: which yet are with much sweat to be searched out
items.note: Even what is handed down must be searched out with labour; it is not given openly.

items.quote: Without paines-taking none is fit to injoy that Art.
items.note: The margin note makes labour the condition for enjoying the Art.

items.name: Men of shallow judgement
items.quote: that he approveth of no sort of Physitians, but that he would professe himselfe to be the sole and onely Physitian in all the world
items.note: A view the author reports from men of shallow judgement in order to reject it.

items.quote: he only condemns the common rable of Physitians who are altogether ignorant both of Theory & Practice
items.note: The author's own account of whom Paracelsus condemns: only physicians ignorant of both theory and practice.

items.quote: Nor truely are they to be accounted Physitians, who Verbally and Syllogistically onely make a great flourish of Physick, but doe no cures at all
items.note: Physicians who only argue and do no cures are not physicians in the author's view.

items.quote: they had rather let their Patients perish then make use of his prescriptions
items.note: Opponents of Theophrastus refuse his prescriptions out of hostility; the text names him both Paracelsus and Theophrastus in this paragraph.

items.quote: the better they are, the more doe they undervalue them
items.note: His medicines are despised for fear their effect would harm the opponents' repute.

items.name: Censurers of Theophrastus
items.quote: falsly charge the genuine Chymists that they have lost the right method
items.note: The charge of the 'fallacious Medodists' against the Chymists, reported in order to be rejected.

items.quote: tis plaine to those that have their understanding inlightned
items.note: What is plain is plain only to readers with an enlightened understanding.

items.quote: Paracelsus observed onely that method that was agreeable to Reason and Experience
items.note: The author holds that Paracelsus kept a method grounded in reason and experience.

items.quote: we are not so much to regard by whom, as what it is that is spoken
items.note: Truth is to be preferred to any man's authority.

items.quote: True Method consisteth in the knowledg of the Disease, and the Cure of it
items.note: The text says what true Method means: knowing the disease and curing it with food and fitting medicines.

items.name: Wimpeneus
items.quote: Wimpeneus learnedly sheweth that greatest and most grievous Diseases now a dayes are in three respects cured by the Paracelsians
items.note: Wimpeneus is the named source for the three respects that follow.

items.quote: in three respects
items.note: Announces a numbered set of three reasons, taken up as First, Secondly, Thirdly in CH5.32, CH5.45, CH5.46.

items.quote: First, Because the Diseases are more perfectly known
items.note: First of the three respects: better knowledge of diseases.

items.quote: those that sprang from Tartar cleaving to any part could not be cured, because it cannot be referred to any of those four humours
items.note: Diseases from Tartar fall outside the four humours and so were not curable before.

items.quote: And since we are here fallen upon Tartar I will speak a little more of it.
items.note: Announces a digression on Tartar, closed at CH5.44.

items.quote: The first Ens or Being toward life
items.note: The text glosses Ens as Being; the first Ens is that from which the body has nourishment.

items.quote: by the Archaeus, or digestion of the Stomack
items.note: The text glosses the Archaeus here as the digestion of the stomach.

items.quote: it's separation, and generation of separation
items.note: The first Ens arises from the last matter of the meat by separation.

items.quote: 'Tis reduc'd unto Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt, as is plain in the three chief Emunctories
items.note: Nourishment is reduced into three: Sulphur, Mercury, Salt, shown by three outlets of the body.

items.quote: the superfluity of Salt is separated by the Urine, that of Sulphure is divided and purged through the Entrals
items.note: Excess Salt leaves by urine, excess Sulphur through the bowels.

items.quote: if there be too much of it passeth through the pores by sweat
items.note: Excess Mercury, the moisture of what nourishes, leaves by sweat.

items.quote: Every member hath its own proper digestion, seperation, emunctory, excrement in it selfe.
items.note: Each member has its own digestion, separation and outlet.

items.quote: The first digestion of the stomack is not digestion, but apparation for the digestions of the particular members.
items.note: The note denies that the stomach's first digestion is digestion, while CH5.33 glosses the Archaeus as the digestion of the stomach.

items.quote: Whatsoever we eat and drink hath in it a mucilagenous, clayish, and sandy Tartar hurtful to our Health
items.note: All food and drink carries Tartar.

items.quote: the Stomack which is the instrument of Mans Archaeus, or the Internal, innate Chymist which God hath planted in Man
items.note: The Archaeus is called the internal, innate Chymist planted in man; the stomach is its instrument.

items.quote: it seperateth that which is impure, dreggy, and Tartarous from the pure Nourishment
items.note: The stomach separates impure from pure as soon as it takes anything in.

items.quote: If the Stomack be weak and feeble the impure also is sent through the Mesaraick veins to the Liver, and there separated and digested the second time
items.note: A weak stomach passes the impure on to the liver for a second separation.

items.quote: seperateth the pure from the impure, viz. the Rubie from the Chrystall
items.note: Pure and impure are given the names of stones, Rubie and Chrystall; the text itself glosses them.

items.quote: The Rubie is the nourishment of all the members
items.note: The text says what the Rubie is.

items.quote: the Christall or that which is not the nourishment it sendeth to the reines
items.note: The text says the Christall is what is not nourishment, sent to the kidneys.

items.quote: this is urine, which is nothing else but the Salt pressed out of the Mercurialls, forced into resolution by the violence of separation
items.note: Urine is defined as Salt pressed out of the Mercurialls by separation.

items.quote: the Spirit of the Salt coming between by the power of predestination, it is coagulated into Sand or Tartar, either cloddy or mucilaginous
items.note: When the liver separates badly, the Spirit of the Salt coagulates the matter in the kidneys into sand or Tartar.

items.quote: the second which is of the stomack into haile; the third of the kidneys and bladder into a little stone
items.what: the first, second and third separation of Tartar
items.note: The note numbers three separations of Tartar and names their products: mosse, haile, stone.

items.quote: The first separation of Tartar, which is by the Live
items.note: The note puts the liver's separation first and the stomach's second; CH5.34 has the stomach separate first and the liver the second time. A gap follows the quoted words.

items.quote: Every Man hath mosse & haile, but not a stone in him.
items.note: Mosse and haile are in every man; the stone is not.

items.quote: Tartar therefore is the excrement of meat and drink, which by the spirit of Salt is coagulated in Man
items.note: The text states what Tartar is.

items.quote: four kinds of Tartar, the stone of the bladder, the Sand of the Kidneys, the clods or gobbets, as also the Slime or lutous matter of the stomack
items.note: Four kinds named by where and how they lodge in the body.

items.quote: with many other diseases which the Ancients knew not
items.note: The Ancients did not know these diseases.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: Paracelsus distinguisheth Tartar into that which is strange or forraine proceeding from meat and drink, and that which is innate of the cruor or hereditary blood
items.note: Paracelsus' twofold division of Tartar: foreign from food, innate from hereditary blood.

items.quote: onely by the Quint-Essence of Gold which reneweth the whole body
items.note: Innate Tartar is curable only by the Quint-Essence of Gold; whether this is Croll's or Paracelsus' claim the sentence does not show.

items.quote: Tartar therefore or the Naturall superfluity (the mucilage of Salt) is the mother of almost all diseases of all coagulate bodies
items.note: Tartar glossed as the natural superfluity, the mucilage of Salt.

items.quote: hath Poyson or a Tartarous Mucilaginous Impurity hard by or close unto the medicine or Physick thereof
items.note: By divine ordination every food carries poison beside its medicine; Poyson is glossed as Tartarous impurity.

items.name: Paracels
items.quote: Paracels saith that the Matter, viz. the Tartar of diseases is twofold
items.note: The note gives Paracelsus' twofold division: Bolous and Viscous.

items.quote: Bolous, such as in milk meats, fish, and flesh
items.note: Two named kinds of the matter of diseases, sorted by food.

items.quote: There are four sorts of Tartar, springing from the fourfold fruits of the Elements by which we are nourished.
items.note: Announces four sorts by source, listed CH5.39 to CH5.42.

items.quote: The first sort ariseth from the use of those things which grow in the Earth
items.note: First sort: from what grows in the earth.

items.quote: The second cometh from the nourishment which we have from the Water
items.note: Second sort: from water foods.

items.quote: The third is in the Flesh of Beasts and Fowles.
items.note: Third sort: from flesh; no element is named for it.

items.quote: The fourth from the Firmament, which is most like to the Spirit of wine in its subtilty
items.note: Fourth sort: from the Firmament, the subtlest and strongest.

items.quote: if the Aire be infected by the vapours of the Earth, and Water, and Firmament, afterward it affecteth us also
items.note: Infected air carries the fourth sort to us.

items.quote: which diseases proceeding from the impressions of the Stars the universall medicine powerfull expelleth
items.note: Astral diseases are expelled by the universal medicine, named but not described here.

items.quote: Those four kinds of Tartar shew themselves in the Urine, and are judged of by the art of separation
items.note: Diagnosis: the kind of Tartar is judged in the urine by the art of separation.

items.quote: He that knoweth what sort of food any one eateth, may also know his disease
items.note: Food and disease can each be known from the other.

items.quote: The disease is cured by the same Element that was the cause of it.
items.note: Cure by the same element that caused the disease.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: which Paracelsus comprehendeth under the name of Poyson and Tartar
items.note: Paracelsus' names for the excrements of meat and drink: Poyson and Tartar.

items.quote: Choller and Melancholly had long since been rooted out of the Physitians Garden
items.note: Had Galen and his followers known Tartar, the humoral terms would be gone.

items.quote: He that knoweth not this Tartarous matter of diseases which proceedeth from the excrementitious superfluities of meat and drink, cannot possibly understand how the Author of diseases afflicteth us
items.note: Knowing Tartar is needed to understand how disease harms us; the Author of diseases is not named.

items.quote: by destroying the frame of the little world
items.note: Man is called the little world.

items.quote: our Naturall Heat, or the microcosmicall heat of the Sun and Moon that is in us
items.note: Natural heat is glossed as the heat of Sun and Moon within us, which digests the nutriment.

items.quote: then it must be strengthned by its like, that is, by the macrocosmicall Heat of Sun and Moon, if it could be got
items.note: Weak inner heat is strengthened by its like in the great world.

items.quote: even the most simple matter which the most Great God generated of the spirit of the world (one and the same with the spirit of our body)
items.note: A matter is pointed to but not named; the text says only what it is made of and what it is for.

items.quote: is deduced by art into act, viz. turned into such a simple spirit as is the spirit of our life, which is done by resolution and conjuction with the Nutriment
items.note: Things holding the power of Sun and Moon are turned by art into a simple spirit, by resolution and conjunction with nutriment.

items.quote: The Vitall spirit in Man and the Elementall is but one spirit.
items.note: The note makes the vital and the elemental spirit one.

items.quote: then the excrements stay in the Chylus, and cause stomachall diseases in the stomack, Jecorall in the liver
items.note: When the separating Archaeus fails, excrements stay and breed diseases by place.

items.quote: Tartar differeth according to the places of the bodies pores and passages
items.what: Tartar by places of the body
items.note: Tartar is distinguished by where it lodges.

items.quote: Therefore the Archaeus of the stomack must destroy the Tartar of the Elements least it be turned into the Tartar of Man
items.note: Two Tartars named: of the Elements and of Man.

items.quote: the spirit of the Sun which is Lord and Master of coagulation in various subjects will breed the Stone
items.note: The spirit of the Sun is made lord of coagulation; the Stone here is the bodily stone.

items.quote: So much for Tartar.
items.note: Closes the digression announced at CH5.32.

items.quote: Secondly, Because we have more perfect medicines now then heretofore, that is to say, of Mineralls
items.note: Second respect: better medicines, of minerals.

items.quote: those skilfull Chymists the Sons of Cadmus
items.note: The Chymists are given a figurative name the text does not explain.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: Paracelsus would have a steely medicine applied as proper for an iron disease
items.note: Paracelsus' rule of like for like: a steely medicine for an iron disease.

items.quote: extream diseases call for extream remedies
items.note: Hard diseases need hard remedies, as a knotty piece needs hard wedges.

items.quote: Thirdly, Because now the Harmony between the great and little world is made so plaine
items.note: Third respect: the harmony of great and little world shows which medicine suits which member.

items.quote: as Silver, Saphir, Vitrioll, Emeralds, for the braine; for the heart, Gold, Pearles, Saffron; for the lungs, Brimstone
items.note: Medicines matched to members.

items.quote: Whereas Paracelsus offendeth Galen, Galen did the same to others
items.note: Disagreement is common among all physicians, not peculiar to Paracelsus.

items.name: Schekius; Fuchsius
items.quote: As between Schekius and Fuchsius about the continent Cause of diseases.
items.note: Named physicians in dispute.

items.name: Argenterius; Fernelius
items.quote: Between Argenterius and Fernelius about Agues and Fevers.
items.note: Named physicians in dispute.

items.name: Galen; Rondeletius
items.quote: Between Galen and Rondeletius concerning the Palsie, Epilepsie and Stone.
items.note: Named physicians in dispute.

items.name: Francaneianus; Rondelatius; Fallopius
items.quote: Between Francaneianus, Rondelatius and Fallopius about the French Pox.
items.note: Named physicians in dispute.

items.name: Altomarus; Fernelius
items.quote: Between Altomarus and Fernelius concerning the Gout.
items.note: Named physicians in dispute.

items.name: Agryppa
items.quote: You may find more jarring in opinions in Agryppa de vanit te Scientia
items.note: The note points to a writing by Agryppa for more disagreements; a gap follows the title.

items.quote: How many millions, according to the disagreeing and jarring method of these men, will still perish
items.note: The physicians' disputes cost lives.

items.quote: I willingly passe by the Herbarists, who commonly squabble and raile at one another with endlesse jangling about the Wool of Plants
items.note: The herbalists are passed over as quarrelsome.

items.quote: I exhort and admonish all Students of Hippocraticall and Galenicall Physick, in whom the Philosophicall veine is yet warme
items.note: The admonition is addressed to students of the old physic.

items.quote: what our industry hath found out should not shut the door against that of the Ancients
items.note: New finding does not exclude the Ancients.

items.quote: spend some time in reading the works of this new Phylosopher and Physitian, not superficially and prefunctorily, but with greatest diligence and attention of mind
items.note: Paracelsus is to be read with great diligence.

items.quote: we are to imitate the experience and industry of the Bees
items.note: Reading is likened to bees segregating the best from the worst; a figure for selective reading.

items.quote: I doe not so far perswade men that they should so adore every thing of Paracelsus
items.note: Paracelsus is not to be taken as Gospel-Oracles.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: he himselfe hath recanted something of his over hasty writings
items.note: Paracelsus himself retracted some writings.

items.quote: the diligent and accurate reading of him may give us greater light, and be no small advantage to us for the more intimate and right understanding of Hippocrates his works
items.note: Reading Paracelsus helps the understanding of Hippocrates.

items.quote: They are not to be praised who rashly condemn all that Paracelsus hath written, when yet they have not read so much as his marginall notes
items.note: His condemners have not read him, or understand not a third part.

items.quote: throw away the kernell and pick up onely the husks of Phylosophers
items.note: Kernel and husk: the philosophers' writings have an inner and an outer part.

items.quote: for the spirit, that ye may understand the dead letter of Theophrastus, and the Phylosophers
items.note: Spirit set against dead letter: the letter of the writings is not their sense.

items.quote: His works which were Printed for the publick good, by the incouragement and at the cost of that most Renowned and Reverend Ernestus Prince Elector of Coleine
items.note: Paracelsus' printed works and their patron are named.

items.name: his adversaries
items.quote: have given occasion to his adversaries to charge him with implicite and evident contradiction
items.note: The adversaries' charge of contradiction, which the author answers by the magical style.

items.quote: to the unskilfull and unlearned he wrote in a Magicall stile; not for the vulgar sort, but for himselfe and the understanding children of Wisdome trained up in the School of Magick
items.note: Paracelsus wrote in a magical style, meant only for the children of Wisdom.

items.quote: not for the Sophisticall Alchymists, such as are bewitch'd with a greedy desire of Gold
items.note: Readers excluded: the gold-greedy alchemists.

items.quote: incensed with a righteous hatred against some most wretched, wicked, inhumane Physitians and Druggists of his time
items.note: A further reason for his style: hatred of physicians who sought to poison him.

items.quote: those circumforanceous and vulgar Alchymists would have surpassed all other Physitians, and prostituted the Art
items.note: Had he written more plainly, vulgar alchemists would have abused the Art; the reason for not writing plainly.

items.quote: He concealed his mysteries under vulgar and various names
items.note: Stated: his mysteries are hidden under ordinary and varied names.

items.quote: we must not take the similitudes for the truth it selfe, or that which is intended by them
items.note: The text says its similitudes are not meant plainly.

items.quote: the Physicall Secrets, that is, the hidden power of God, or the Magicall WORDS in Paracelsus
items.note: The text glosses the Physical Secrets as the hidden power of God, or the magical words.

items.quote: they need and require a Delian swimmer, a most acute and sharp wit, a Magicall Understanding, even that purified eye of the Mind
items.note: Few understand; a special reader is needed to search out the secret mysteries.

items.quote: every were I mean that which is True and lawfull
items.note: The author says what he means by Magick; a gap stands inside the word Magick before the quote.

items.quote: which is fit for none but Vulcan, and deserveth to be burned
items.note: Witchcraft is rejected and set apart from true Magick.

items.quote: the absolute perfection of the whole most noble Phylosophy, the chiefest Wisdome of Gods works and the plenary knowledge of occult Nature
items.note: What true Magick is.

items.quote: by a fit application of Agents and Patients, observing the consent and dissent of things
items.note: How Magick works its wonders.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: Paracelsus hath joyned the exercetation of either medicine together, as well that of Physick as of Chyrurgie, in imitation and after the example of Great Hippocrates
items.note: Paracelsus joins physic and surgery, following Hippocrates.

items.quote: a twofold Medicine, Physicall or the knowledge of all diseases, and Chyrurgicall or the curing of the same
items.note: The text says what Physicall and Chyrurgicall medicine mean.

items.quote: it is necessary that every Surgeon should be a Physician, and every Physitian a Chyrurgion
items.note: The two must be one person.

items.quote: that there may be a sound Bridgroom for a sound Bride
items.note: A marriage figure for the union of physic and surgery.

items.quote: their preparations and compositions made by the Physitian himselfe, and not carelesly left to others
items.note: The physician prepares his own medicines.

items.quote: by their own hand to prepare the medicaments which they know, to seperate and purge them from their poyson and dreggs, to reduce them to their pure simplicity
items.note: Preparation: separate, purge of poison and dregs, reduce to pure simplicity.

items.quote: For the Bad and Good are mixt together, neither is Sugar free from faeculent impurity, nor is honey voyd of a venemous bitternesse
items.note: Every substance mixes good and bad, hence the need of separation.

items.quote: judgement without practice is altogether barren and fruitlesse
items.note: Theory and practice both needed.

items.quote: Physick is learned by the labour of the hands and practicall working or making it up, when the Fire discovereth new and most pleasant Remedies continually
items.note: Physic learned by handwork at the fire.

items.quote: which Nature dayly more and more purgeth from their superfluities, and then delivereth them to her Servant to make them up
items.note: Nature purges remedies and hands them to her Servant; matches the chapter title's Natures Minister.

items.quote: will not become schollers and school-boyes againe, to dig they are ashamed
items.note: The great doctors refuse to learn handwork.

items.quote: because they can prepare their medicines but onely with their Reason, not at all with their hand
items.note: Rational physicians fail at the sickbed for lack of handwork.

items.quote: Yet here I will by no means undertake to defend them, who reteining the works of Hippocrates and of the Ancients, yet boast themselves to be the Schollers of Paracelsus
items.note: The author disowns false followers of Paracelsus.

items.quote: Experience, without Phylosophy the mother of Experience is uncertaine.
items.note: Philosophy is called the mother of experience.

items.quote: These Receits being lost by chance, all the Wisdome vanisheth from them
items.note: Those relying on receipts lose all when the receipts are lost.

items.quote: There are also false and lying Theophrasteans prophaning by their avarice and timerity that Divine Physick
items.note: False Theophrasteans profane the Divine Physick.

items.quote: who under disguised names vaunt and vapour that they make use of Theophrastus his medicines
items.note: They claim his medicines under disguised names.

items.quote: before they scarce know how to put fire into the furnace
items.note: They attempt great cures without knowing the furnace.

items.quote: cure the party and his disease at once with a turse of the Church-yard
items.note: An ironic figure: the cure is the patient's death.

items.quote: These men get their knowledge piece-meale out of men, & gaine their experience by the death of others
items.note: The false practitioners learn by others' deaths.

items.quote: all the Medicines both of the Arabians and Grecians, are desperate and without hope of doing any good
items.note: In great diseases the old medicines fail.

items.quote: doe sometime exceed many Galenists in many great and perilous diseases
items.note: The author concedes that the adulterous Theophrasteans sometimes outdo Galenists.

items.quote: yet no conscientious man will ever approve their uncertaine, bold, rash, dangerous, impious practice of Physick
items.note: Yet their practice is condemned.

items.quote: No rabble of Physitians in the City is more numerous then these.
items.note: The note says these are the most numerous in the city.
